Where it began

Michael Hussey was born in Perth on 27 May 1975 and went to school in the city's northern suburbs. He trained to be a science teacher before cricket took over, and a scholarship to the Australian Cricket Academy put him alongside Brett Lee and Jason Gillespie. His younger brother, David, also went on to play for Victoria and for Australia.

Then came a very long apprenticeship. He played for Western Australia and spent several seasons in England with Northamptonshire, where he made 329 not out in 2001 and topped it with 331 not out at Taunton two years later. By the time Australia picked him for a Test he had already scored 15,313 first-class runs.

The player

His first Test came in November 2005 at Brisbane, when he was already 30. Hundreds in his second and third Tests made sure he stayed, and in April 2006 he reached 1,000 Test runs after just 166 days, faster than anyone before him.

He played 79 Tests between 2005 and 2013, scoring 6,235 runs at 51.53 with 19 hundreds and 29 fifties, and held 85 catches. His best was 195 against England at Brisbane in the 2010–11 Ashes, made during a stand of 307 with Brad Haddin. In the 5–0 Ashes win of 2006–07 he averaged over a hundred, and in the 2009 Ashes his 121 at The Oval came at just the right moment.

What made him special

Hussey was at his best when things were going wrong. Batting down the order, he had a gift for staying in while the tail held on at the other end. He added 107 for the last wicket with Glenn McGrath, 320 with Gillespie, who had come in as nightwatchman, and an unbeaten 134 at Sydney with Peter Siddle in support turned a losing Test into a win against Pakistan.

His bowling was a gentler business. He sent down the odd spell of medium pace, usually to give the quicker men a breather, and collected seven Test wickets. His best figures, one for none, sound rather grand.

Away from the middle

His deep knowledge of the game earned him the nickname Mr Cricket, though it was never a name he much cared for himself. He was a big part of Chennai's IPL side, winning the title with them in 2010, and later captained Sydney Thunder to the Big Bash title before he finished playing after the 2015–16 season.

Since then he has coached batsmen for Australia, England and Chennai, commentated, and been Director of Cricket at Sydney Thunder. His autobiography, Underneath the Southern Cross, appeared in 2013, and he entered the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame at the 2023 Boxing Day Test.

And finally

Playing for Australia A, he once heard Allan Border suggest, as a joke, that he could get some batting practice by staying in the nets for six hours. Hussey took him at his word and did exactly that. It explains a good deal about the 15,313 runs.
